vignette:
Rangi Tuilagi is a 51-year-old Samoan-American man who has worked as a welder for nearly two decades, a trade he learned from his father and has always taken quiet pride in. He is married, the father of three adult children, and until fourteen months ago described himself as someone who had never given much thought to his own mortality. That changed on a Tuesday evening in late autumn when a drunk driver ran a red light at approximately fifty miles per hour and struck the driver's side of Rangi's pickup truck. The impact crumpled the door inward against his left shoulder and hip, pinned him at an angle with his torso twisted hard to the right, and left him conscious and unable to move while fuel leaked and other drivers shouted from the roadside. Paramedics noted a strong smell of alcohol emanating from the other vehicle when they arrived. Rangi sustained fractures to his left clavicle and two ribs, and he remained in that wrenched, compressed position for nearly forty minutes before rescue workers could extract him.

In the weeks following his discharge from hospital, Rangi found that the event did not stay in the past where he expected it to go. Instead, it returned to him with a quality he struggled to describe to his wife, Leilani - not like remembering, he told her, but like being pulled back inside it. When the memories arrived they were not visual alone. He could smell the alcohol again, sharp and unmistakable, a smell that now reached him across distances that should have been safe: a colleague cracking open a beer at a weekend barbecue, the cleaning aisle at the hardware store, even Leilani's glass of wine at the dinner table. Each time, the memory did not merely surface - it flooded him, complete and simultaneous across every sense, as though the intervening months had not existed. What frightened Rangi most in these moments was what happened to his body. He would feel his torso twist involuntarily into that same compressed angle, his left shoulder pulling tight, and the pain - a dull, crushing ache along his clavicle and down his ribs - would return with a fidelity he could not explain and could not dismiss. He had come to believe, with a certainty he found difficult to articulate but impossible to shake, that his body had not fully left the wreckage.

The sounds of traffic became their own category of difficulty. Rangi works in a fabrication yard situated alongside a busy arterial road, and the ambient noise of passing vehicles - the particular percussion of trucks decelerating, the sudden sharp note of brakes, the low rumble of engines idling close - punctuated his shifts in ways that made sustained concentration increasingly hard. He began wearing his hearing protection earlier in the day than required and keeping it on during breaks, a habit his foreman initially said nothing about but eventually raised with him. Driving himself to work, which had once been forty unremarkable minutes each way, became something he endured rather than performed. He stopped using the highway and added twenty minutes to his commute on surface streets, and then, over the following months, began asking Leilani to drive him when her schedule allowed. She had accommodated this without complaint, but Rangi was aware that it had reorganised her mornings in ways she had not signed up for, and the awareness sat heavily with him.

He had not sought help immediately. He had told himself, and believed for a time, that the body heals and the mind follows. But fourteen months on, the intrusions had not diminished, the smell of alcohol remained a reliable door back into the cab of his truck, and a near-miss in the fabrication yard parking lot - another vehicle reversing too fast, nothing serious - had left him shaking for the remainder of the shift and sleepless for three nights afterward. It was Leilani who finally said, plainly and without accusation, that she did not recognise the man who flinched at wine glasses. Rangi made the appointment the following morning. He arrived hoping, above everything else, to find a way to inhabit his own body again without it insisting, against all evidence, that the accident was still happening.
